questions.problem: $\int (4-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =4x-\frac{3}{2}(-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)+C \\  & =4x+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]+C \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

 

Letting $\theta =4x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡8x{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(1-1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

A={\int }_{0}^{\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x.

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4}).\end{aligned}

questions.problem: $\int ({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate 
${\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =2x$, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡2x=2[\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi +2\pi -\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2{\pi }^{3}]-[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi +\pi -\frac{1}{3}{\pi }^{3}] \\  & =2\pi -\frac{8{\pi }^{3}}{3}-\pi +\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\pi -\frac{7{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\pi -7{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi (3-7{\pi }^{2})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{sin}^{2}⁡x+11{cos}^{2}⁡x & =5{sin}^{2}⁡x+5{cos}^{2}⁡x+6{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =5({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+6{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =5+6{cos}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(5+6{cos}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[5+6\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8+3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(8x+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[8\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})]-[8(0)+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))] \\  & =[4\pi +\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )]-[0+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =[4\pi +\frac{3}{2}(0)]-[0+\frac{3}{2}(0)] \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

A={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-2{sin}^{2}⁡x+2x)\,\text{d}x.

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1=-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-2{sin}^{2}⁡x+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x+{x}^{2})|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi -\pi +{\pi }^{2}]-[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{{2}^{2}}] \\  & =-\pi +{\pi }^{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{4{\pi }^{2}-4\pi -{\pi }^{2}+2\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3{\pi }^{2}-2\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi (3\pi -2)}{4}\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we have

$$
6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{4})=3(1-cos\,(\frac{x}{2})).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\,[6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{4})-3+3cos\,(\frac{x}{2})+x]dx & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\,[3-3cos\,(\frac{x}{2})-3+3cos\,(\frac{x}{2})+x]dx \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x\,dx \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{(2\pi )^{2}-{\pi }^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Calculate
$\int 6{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =3x$, we have

$$
2{sin}^{2}⁡3x=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\cdot 2{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 3(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =3x-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡6x}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2})-2{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}) & =1-{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2})-2{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}) \\  & =1-3{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{3x}{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))={sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(1-3{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{3x}{2}))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(1-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{2}x)\,|}_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3})-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2\pi }{3}]-[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}] \\  & =[0-\frac{\pi }{3}]-[0-\frac{\pi }{6}] \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta} =2\sin \theta \cos \theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) = \sin{\theta}\cos{\theta}.
$$

 

Letting $\theta= \dfrac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{1}{2} \sin \left(2\cdot \dfrac{x}{2} \right) &= \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\[5pt]
\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x	&= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos  \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right).
  }
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C.	
	}
$$

$$
\cos^2\theta -\sin^2\theta=\cos 2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$ gives

$$
\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x = \cos 6x,
$$

and therefore,

$$

	}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\cos^2{x}$ term, given by

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \cos^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int ( \cos {2x} +1) \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
                                                                 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} +x\right) + C\[5pt]
								&= \dfrac{1}{4}\sin {2x} +\dfrac{1}{2}x + C.
								
	}
$$
